title: Middle of the Parade
story: A town parade is a line of floats. Each driver only knows which float is right behind them. Nobody has the full list or knows how long the parade is.
The TV crew wants to film from the middle float. Starting at the lead float and following "who is behind you", find it.
task: Write middleFloat(head). head is the first node of a linked list (each node has val and next). Return the middle node.

With an odd number of floats there is one middle. With an even number there are two; return the second. The tests read the list from the node you return to the end, so the middle of [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] shows as [3, 4, 5].
constraints: Float ids are integers and may repeat.
Return a node from the list you were given; do not build a new list.

examples.explanation: Five floats. The third, 6, has two ahead and two behind. From 6 the parade reads 6, 2, 9.
Four floats, so 3 and 6 are both in the middle. The rule picks the second, 6. Returning 3 would show [3, 6, 2] and fail.

hints: Two friends start at the lead float. One walks one float at a time, the other two at a time. Where is the slow one when the fast one runs out of parade?
The fast walker covers twice the slow one's distance. So when the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is halfway.
Watch the stopping rule. Try 2 floats and 4 floats and check that the slow walker stops on the second middle.
Start slow and fast at head. While fast and fast.next both exist, move slow one step and fast two. Return slow.
bruteForce: Walk the parade once to count the floats, n. Walk again from the start and stop after n / 2 steps (rounded down).

That is O(n) and correct, but takes two passes. The trick here finds the middle in one pass without knowing n, which you need when the list is read once, like a stream, or inside a bigger list algorithm.

js: * function ListNode(val, next) { this.val = val; this.next = next; }
* ListNode is already defined for you.
* @return {ListNode} the middle float (the second one if there are two)

tests.note: two floats: the second is the middle
even length: picking the first middle fails here

js: // fast moves 2 steps for every 1 step of slow
py: # fast moves 2 steps for every 1 step of slow
while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
walkthrough: You do not need the length. Send two pointers down the list at different speeds; when the fast one runs out, the slow one is halfway.
• slow = 8, fast = 8. fast has a next, so move: slow = 3, fast = 6.
• fast = 6 has a next, so move: slow = 6, fast = 9.

With 8 → 3 → 6 → 2: after one move slow = 3, fast = 6; after the second slow = 6, fast = null. The loop stops and slow sits on the second middle, 6. For the first middle, stop one step earlier by checking fast.next.next.
solution.timeWhy: fast crosses the list once; slow makes half as many steps.
solution.takeaway: Fast and slow pointers find positions defined by the length (the middle, a third of the way) in one pass without counting. They also split a list in half for merge sort and palindrome checks.
